Save this as a new object called `wbns_00`. Use `dim()` to print the number of rows and columns to verify the import. ::: ::: callout-tip If you get an error like `No such file`, double-check: (1) you opened your `.Rproj` before running code, (2) the folder names in `here()` match your folders exactly, and (3) the file name, including `.rds`, is spelled exactly right. ::: ### Filtering to Your Target Subpopulation To implement an asset-focused analysis, we must first isolate the subpopulation relevant to your project using [`filter()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/21_Data_transformation_rows/Data_transformation_rows.html#/filter-1). 1. Your filter must match the category spelling exactly, including capital letters. 2. Write your filter using the conditions in your project's tab below. Remember from [Lesson 23](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/23_Data_transformation_advanced/Data_transformation_advanced.html#/filtering-with-and-criteria-12): `&` means **both** conditions must be true, and `|` means **at least one** must be true. Use parentheses to group the "or" part. 3. Save the result as `wbns_01_pop`. 4. Use [`dim()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/16_Piping/Piping.html#/two-types-of-pipes-you-might-see) on `wbns_00` and on `wbns_01_pop` to compare the number of rows before and after filtering. ::: {.panel-tabset group="project"} #### Project 1 Keep respondents who are under 100% of the FPL **and** received free groceries or meals in the past 12 months: - Under 100% FPL: `FPL_LT50` **or** `FPL50_100` equals `"Yes"` - **and** received free groceries or meals: **any** of `Q25`, `Q25A`, `Q26`, or `Q26A` equals `"Yes"` Look these four questions up in the questionnaire: `Q25` and `Q26` ask about free groceries and free meals in the past 30 days, and `Q25A` and `Q26A` follow up with people who said no. These are exactly the people who were asked the `Q26D` ease-of-access questions. The structure of your filter will be: `(FPL condition | FPL condition) & (Q25 condition | Q25A condition | Q26 condition | Q26A condition)`. #### Project 2 Keep respondents who identify as LGBTQ **and** who have a healthcare provider: - `LGBTQ` equals `"Yes"` - **and** `Q108` was **not** answered `"No"` For the second condition, use [`filter_out()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/21_Data_transformation_rows/Data_transformation_rows.html#/filter_out-new-companion-to-filter) from Lesson 25 instead of `!=`. If you chose a different population (for example, using `Q70F`), write out your conditions in words first, then translate them into code. #### Project 3 Keep respondents with at least one child aged 5-18 in the household **and** who are under 100% of the FPL: - `ANY_CHILDHH_5_18` equals `"Yes"` - **and** `FPL_LT50` **or** `FPL50_100` equals `"Yes"` The structure of your filter will be: `ANY_CHILDHH_5_18 condition & (FPL condition | FPL condition)`. ::: ::: callout-important #### Task Write a pipeline that filters the dataset down to your specific population of interest. Save this as a new object called `wbns_01_pop`. Use `dim()` to print the number of rows before and after filtering to verify the operation. ::: ::: callout-caution Please make sure you are referencing the PDF with the questionnaire when filtering out your population. There are important descriptions and caveats in the questionnaire! ::: ### Selecting Project Variables Your dataset contains hundreds of variables. For project clarity, reduce your data frame to only the variables in the informational table above. 1. Make a list of the variables you need from the table: the respondent ID variable (find its name in the codebook), your **population** variables, your **main** variables, and the **additional** variables. 2. *Optional:* If you are interested in other variables, add 0-3 more that are not listed. 3. Use [`select()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/22_Data_transformation_columns/Data_transformation_columns.html#/subsetting-columns-using-select) to keep only those variables. You can type each name, or use a helper from Lesson 23 like `starts_with("Q26D")` to grab a group of similarly named variables at once. 4. Save the result as `wbns_02_pop_vars`. 5. Use [`dim()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/16_Piping/Piping.html#/two-types-of-pipes-you-might-see) on `wbns_01_pop` and on `wbns_02_pop_vars`. The number of rows should stay the same, and the number of columns should drop. ::: callout-important #### Task Use `select()` to keep the variables relevant to your project. Save this as a new object called `wbns_02_pop_vars`. Use `dim()` to print the number of columns before and after selecting to verify the operation. ::: ### Rename variables for clarity Most variables in the WBNS dataset are named after their survey question code (e.g. `Q108B_2`), which isn't very informative on its own and is easy to mix up as your pipeline grows. Renaming your variables to short, descriptive names now will make the rest of your code (and your missing data plots) easier to read and less error-prone. 1. Use [`rename()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/22_Data_transformation_columns/Data_transformation_columns.html#/renaming-with-rename) with the pattern `new_name = old_name`. 2. Rename your **main** variables using the **exact names** in your project's tab below. Labs 3 and 4 use these names. 3. Rename your **additional** variables. Some have names given below. For any listed as "your choice," pick a name that follows these rules: - all lowercase, with words separated by underscores (`_`), and no spaces - short, but describes what the question asks (look it up in the questionnaire!) 4. You do **not** need to rename the ID or population variables. 5. Save this as a new object called `wbns_03_renamed`. Use `glimpse()` to confirm your new variable names. ::: ### Explore missing data Before we change or remove anything, we need to know **how much data is missing, where it is, and why.** We'll use the `naniar` functions from Lesson 24. All of these steps use `wbns_03_renamed`, and none of them create a new dataset. There are **two kinds** of missing data to look for: - **True `NA`s:** R already knows these are missing. The `naniar` functions find them. - **Hidden missing values:** responses like `"Refused"` or `"Don't know"`. R treats these as real categories, so the `naniar` functions will **not** count them. We find these with [`tabyl()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/25_Missing_data_transformations/Missing_data_transformations.html#/warning-on-filter-it-can-silently-drop-your-nas). 1. **Overall missingness.** Use [`n_miss()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/24_Missing_data_summ_viz/Missing_data_summ_viz.html#/missing-values-in-a-dataset) and [`prop_miss()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/24_Missing_data_summ_viz/Missing_data_summ_viz.html#/missing-values-in-a-dataset) on `wbns_03_renamed` to get the total number and proportion of missing cells in your dataset. 2. **Missingness by variable.** Use [`miss_var_summary()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/24_Missing_data_summ_viz/Missing_data_summ_viz.html#/missingness-by-each-variable-for-every-variable), and pipe the result into [`gt()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/24_Missing_data_summ_viz/Missing_data_summ_viz.html#/missingness-by-each-variable-for-every-variable) so it prints as a table. Which variables have the most missing data? 3. **Visualize missingness.** Use [`vis_miss()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/24_Missing_data_summ_viz/Missing_data_summ_viz.html#/vis_miss-visualizing-missing-data-across-the-dataset) to see where the `NA`s are across rows and columns. If your variable names overlap, add the [`theme()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/24_Missing_data_summ_viz/Missing_data_summ_viz.html#/vis_miss-visualizing-missing-data-across-the-dataset) line from Lesson 24 to angle them. 4. **Missing together?** Use [`gg_miss_upset()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/24_Missing_data_summ_viz/Missing_data_summ_viz.html#/gg_miss_upset-missingness-intersections-12) (with `nsets = 10`) to see which variables tend to be missing *together*. 5. **Hidden missing values.** Use `tabyl()` on **each main variable**, one at a time. Write down any categories that really mean "no answer" (for example, `"Refused"` or `"Don't know"`). You'll need this list in the next section. 6. **Explain what you found.** Follow your project's tab below, then write your paragraph. ::: {.panel-tabset group="project"} #### Project 1 The `ease_` items come from `Q26D`, which is only asked of people who received free groceries or meals. Since your population filter already requires that, these items should be mostly complete. If you see a lot of missingness, double-check your filter. You'll also see a lot of missing data in `Q25A` and `Q26A`. That's skip logic, and it doesn't mean "no." `Q25A` (free groceries in the past **12 months**) is only asked of people who said no to `Q25` (free groceries in the past **30 days**). If someone got free groceries in the past 30 days, they obviously got them in the past 12 months, so the survey skips `Q25A`. `Q26A` works the same way with `Q26` for free meals. Your filter already handles this: because it uses `|`, a `"Yes"` on `Q25` keeps the person even when `Q25A` is `NA`. The `ease_` items also have a `"Don't know"` response option. Look for it in your `tabyl()` output! #### Project 2 You kept respondents with a missing `Q108` on purpose (that's why we used [`filter_out()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/21_Data_transformation_rows/Data_transformation_rows.html#/filter_out-new-companion-to-filter)).
